newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Nestle seen boosting '96 profit some 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Nestle seen boosting '96 profit some 10 pct.

text.p: Nestle SA will report a solid gain of around 10 percent in 1996 profit on Wednesday, helped by record turnover last year as volume gains teamed up with the Swiss franc's swoon against major currencies, analysts say.

The median forecast in a survey of 23 analysts by Edinburgh Financial Publishing was for 1996 net profit to rise 10.5 percent to 3.23 billion Swiss francs. It put earnings per share (EPS) at 82 francs, up from 74.4.
Dividends were seen rising to 28 francs per share from 26.5.
"In the last two months of 1996, the dollar and mark gained sharply against the Swiss franc and this clearly helped Nestle," said Alain-Sebastian Oberhuber at UBS.

He upgraded his estimates in January for this reason, seeing 1996 net at 3.16 billion and the dividend at 28 francs. But he said increased marketing costs to push pet food in Germany and the Netherlands would weigh on operating profit gains.
Nestle said in January that 1996 net profit growth should outstrip the 7.1 percent sales gain to 60.5 billion francs.

Chairman Helmut Maucher said in February he expected sales and profit to grow again in 1997 and that profits should rise slightly faster than the average medium-term annual turnover growth rate of seven to nine percent.
UBS has a long-term buy recommendation for Nestle, the world's biggest food company. It said Nestle's estimated 1998 price/earnings ratio of 14.2 is below that of Anglo-Dutch Unilever NV/Plc at 17.8.
"Average annual volume growth of 3.7 percent for the next three years should be higher than at Unilever (three percent) and Danone (2.0 percent)," Oberhuber said in a study.
"We expect rising operating margins again from 1997 and more favourable exchange rates, so we emphasise our long-term buy recommendation."
SBC Warburg also gave Nestle the nod among the big three food companies, but said the others had more potential.

"We maintain the view that Nestle is the better business compared to its European peers, but Unilever and Danone should enjoy the greatest degree of benefit from restructuring in the next two years due to their more significant restructuring programmes," it said in its March report on Swiss equities.
"The recent rally in Danone's shares places the stock valuation almost in line with Nestle's, a position that is not warranted on fundamentals," it added, citing Nestle's superior regional mix.
It put Nestle's 1996 net at 3.20 billion for EPS of 80.9 and saw a dividend of 28.5 francs per share.
SBC Warburg said the market perceived Nestle as hanging on to non-core businesses, in contrast with Unilever, although Nestle had less urgent need to make changes.

Oberhuber at UBS agreed Nestle could make better use of its assets, and suggested it could eventually get rid of its roasted and ground coffee business in the difficult U.S. market and focus instead on its solid instant coffee lines.
Peter Brabeck, set to take over from Helmut Maucher as chief executive in June, could take a more ambitious approach to boosting shareholder value, Oberhuber added.
"I think the company is a bit too big, that it could get rid of some things, products that have low margins and no great potential," he said.
Wilhelm Blaeuer at Pictet & Cie in Geneva said he expected Nestle's overall operating margin to have slipped to 9.4 percent in 1996 from 9.7 percent even as net rises to 3.2 billion.

"I still expect some erosion of operating margins in emerging countries, especially Asian markets," he said, citing the cost of distributing ice cream and the addition of new products with lower margins than Nestle's cash cow, coffee.
He said he was also encouraged that the company was acting to solve problems with its U.S. beverage business that the company acknowledged had weighed on 1996 turnover growth.
"The main problem is simply that in the U.S. you have a long-term switch from bulk coffee and from instant coffee to high-quality, exotic coffee blends," Blaeuer said.
